tip: 'Tô' is casual shorthand for 'estou': 'eu tô precisando' = I'm needing. Formal writing keeps 'estou'.
'Gostar' needs 'de' before the thing you like: it's 'gosto muito de praia', not 'gosto muito praia'.
'Demais' after an adjective means too or excessively: 'salgada demais' = too salty. It follows the word it intensifies.
'Ainda bem' is literally still well and works as thank goodness, so 'ainda bem que deu certo' expresses relief.
After 'gostar', 'de' contracts with a definite article: 'de' + 'o' = 'do', as in 'do trabalho' (not 'de o trabalho').
'De olhos azuis' is how you describe eye color in Portuguese – literally 'of blue eyes'. Same pattern for hair: 'de cabelos pretos'.
'Com licença' is used when you need to get past someone or interrupt politely. It's more common than 'desculpe' for these situations.
'Preferir' = to prefer. Unlike 'gostar' and 'precisar', it does not take 'de': 'preferimos ir' (not 'de ir').
'Perder' means to miss transport, not just to lose: 'perdi o ônibus' = I missed the bus.
'Pois não' is a formal/polite way to say 'how can I help you'. You'll hear it from shopkeepers, receptionists, and servers.
'A gente' means we but takes the same verb form as 'ela', so it is 'a gente gosta', not 'gostamos'.
After 'de' Portuguese uses the plain infinitive where English uses -ing, so 'gosta de ler' means likes reading.
Colors agree with gender and number: 'branco'/'branca'/'brancos'/'brancas'. Some colors don't change: 'laranja', 'rosa', 'violeta'.
'Vi' is the past of 'ver' (to see). 'Vi ela' is informal; formal writing prefers 'eu a vi', but 'vi ela' is standard in speech.
'Quis' is the irregular past of 'querer' (to want): 'eu quis', 'ela quis'. No accent on 'quis'.
'Parecido' takes 'com', not 'a': 'parecida com a mãe' = looks like her mom. Use 'com' for resemblance.
In writing, only the circumflex separates 'pôde' (was able, past) from 'pode' (can, present), so watch the accent.
'Todo mundo' means everyone but is grammatically singular: 'todo mundo riu' = everyone laughed.
The '-inho' ending softens requests. 'Um minutinho' (a little minute) sounds much more polite than 'um minuto'.
To say the most, use a definite article with 'mais': 'a profissional mais qualificada' = the most qualified professional.
'Nada a ver' is literally nothing to see, but it means nothing to do with it, a common way to reject a claim.
'Valeu' is a very casual way to say thanks in Brazil. It literally comes from 'valer' (to be worth). Informal but used everywhere.
'Nenhum' (none/not any) is stronger than a plain 'não': 'de jeito nenhum' literally means in no way at all.
'Pra' is the everyday spoken contraction of 'para' (for/to). 'É pra já' literally 'it's for now', meaning right away.
'Viu' (literally 'did you see') is added at the end of sentences as a tag question meaning 'okay?' or 'got it?'. Very Brazilian.
'Tá bom' is the casual contraction of 'está bom' – used constantly to mean okay/alright. Also 'tá' for 'está', 'tô' for 'estou'.
'E aí' is a very casual greeting, like hey or what's up. Often followed by 'tudo bem?' or 'tudo certo?'
'Nossa' (short for 'Nossa Senhora' = Our Lady) is one of the most common exclamations in Brazil, used for surprise, shock, or emphasis.
'Que' + a noun makes an exclamation: 'que demora' = what a delay. No article is needed after 'que' here.
'Ir' + an '-ndo' form shows an action underway: 'vou correndo' = I'm off running/rushing, not a plain future.
